facts.text: Ingalls was officially named in 1863 after Eleazer Stillman Ingalls, a local judge who helped organize Menominee County.
The Chicago and North Western Railway arrived in 1872, building a station that linked Ingalls to lumber markets.
Ingalls’ settlement began in the mid‑19th century as part of the broader Menominee County formation from Ontonagon County.
Before European settlers, the area was traditional territory of the Menominee, an Algonquian‑speaking tribe spanning Wisconsin and Michigan.
The Menominee River ran through Ingalls, serving as a key boundary and cultural corridor for Ojibwe and other Indigenous peoples.
Ingalls’ early growth was driven by lumbering and mining interests that attracted settlers to its abundant forests, rivers, and wetlands.
